title: Adaptive Model Pooling for Online Deep Anomaly Detection from a Complex Evolving Data Stream

problem.claim: Online anomaly detection must address complex and evolving data streams from IoT devices and cloud-based infrastructures.

gap.claim: Existing online methods struggle with stream complexity, while offline deep anomaly detection methods struggle with evolving data distributions.

contributions.claim: ARCUS is a framework for online deep anomaly detection that can be instantiated with any autoencoder-based deep anomaly detection method.
ARCUS uses adaptive model pooling with concept-driven inference to detect anomalies using a model combination suited to stream complexity.
ARCUS uses drift-aware model pool updates to dynamically adapt the model pool to evolving data streams.

stated_novelty.claim: The framework introduces two techniques described by the authors as novel: concept-driven inference and drift-aware model pool update.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In experiments on ten high-dimensional, concept-drifted data sets, ARCUS improved the anomaly detection accuracy of streaming variants of state-of-the-art autoencoder-based methods by up to 22%.
In the same experiments, ARCUS improved the anomaly detection accuracy of state-of-the-art streaming anomaly detection methods by up to 37%.

narrative_sequence.summary: Online anomaly detection is important for application safety and security but faces complex, evolving streams.
Existing online and offline deep methods inadequately address stream complexity and evolving distributions.
The paper presents ARCUS, an extensible framework for online deep anomaly detection.
ARCUS combines concept-driven inference with drift-aware model pool updates.
Experiments on ten high-dimensional, concept-drifted data sets report accuracy improvements of up to 22% and 37% against two method groups.

source_observation.claim: The framework selects a combination of models suited to current stream complexity and updates the pool as the data stream evolves.

interpretation.claim: Separating adaptation to instantaneous complexity from adaptation to distribution drift may help maintain online detection performance.

application.claim: Online systems facing both heterogeneous complexity and concept drift could use adaptive ensembles with separate inference and pool-update mechanisms.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this separation benefits streams outside the reported setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the ten data sets.
The abstract does not specify evaluation metrics, experimental protocol, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not quantify computational, memory, or latency costs.
